text: José María Gironella Pous (31 December 1917 in Darnius – 3 January 2003 in Arenys de Mar) was a Spanish author best known for his fictional work “The Cypresses Believe in God” (“Los cipreses creen en Dios”), published in Spain in 1953.

José María Gironella’s novel “The Cypresses Believe in God” was translated into English by Harriet de Onís in 1955. It is a two-part novel and the first of four, written from a Roman Catholic viewpoint by a Catholic author educated in a seminary, yet notable for its even-handedness.

José María Gironella’s novel “The Cypresses Believe in God” is set in Girona, a city in eastern Catalonia, and follows a family from 1931 until the Spanish Civil War breaks out in 1936. Its protagonist is the son of an atheist from Madrid, whose father is married to a devout Basque woman, and who has a younger brother and sister also caught up in the conflict.

In the sequel “One Million Dead” (“Un millón de muertos”), translated by Joan MacLean, José María Gironella follows the Alvear family through the war. His next novel, “Peace after War”, was published in English in 1969 and also translated by MacLean, while his fourth novel, Los hombres lloran solos (Men cry alone), has not been translated into English.
“Little Big Man” is a 1964 novel by American author Thomas Berger. It is often described as a satire or parody of the western genre and is a modern example of picaresque fiction.

Thomas Berger drew on a large volume of overlooked first-person primary materials, such as diaries, letters and memoirs, to write “Little Big Man”, a wide-ranging tale that comments on alienation, identity and perceptions of reality.
“Little Big Man” is easily Thomas Berger’s best known work and was made into a popular film by Arthur Penn. It has been called “Berger’s response to the great American myth of the frontier”.
Hugh Gallagher is an author and musician from New York City, and he is best known for his satire across his writing and music.
Hugh Gallagher’s satire includes his band Von Von Von and his award-winning satire on the college application essay, “3A Essay”, which are among his best-known satirical works.
Among Hugh Gallagher’s best-known satirical works is the novel “Teeth”, alongside his band Von Von Von and the award-winning “3A Essay”.
“The Magic Christian” is a 1959 comic novel by American author Terry Southern (1924–1995) about an odd billionaire who spends most of his time playing elaborate practical jokes on people.

Terry Southern’s “The Magic Christian” brought him to the attention of filmmaker Stanley Kubrick, who had received a copy as a gift from Peter Sellers. Kubrick subsequently hired Southern as co-writer for “Dr. Strangelove” (1964) when he decided to make that film a black comedy/satire rather than a straightforward thriller.
In 1969, “The Magic Christian” was made into a film starring Peter Sellers and Ringo Starr; the story was much altered and relocated from New York City to London.
Joanna Russ (February 22, 1937 – April 29, 2011) was an American writer, academic and radical feminist who wrote science fiction, fantasy and feminist literary criticism.
Joanna Russ wrote the feminist literary criticism “How to Suppress Women’s Writing”, the contemporary novel “On Strike Against God”, and the children’s book “Kittatinny”.
Joanna Russ is best known for “The Female Man”, a novel combining utopian fiction and satire, and for the story “When It Changed”.

The Satyricon, or Satyricon “liber” (“The Book of Satyrlike Adventures”), is a Latin work of fiction believed to have been written by Gaius Petronius, although the manuscript tradition identifies the author as Titus Petronius.

The Satyricon is an example of Menippean satire, which is very different from the formal verse satire of Juvenal or Horace. It mixes prose and verse (known as “prosimetrum”), serious and comic elements, and erotic and decadent passages.

Like Apuleius’s “Metamorphoses” (also called “The Golden Ass”), the Satyricon is often described by classical scholars as a “Roman novel”, without necessarily implying continuity with the modern literary form.
Jaroslav Hašek (April 30, 1883 – January 3, 1923) was a Czech writer, humorist, satirist, journalist, bohemian and anarchist, also known as the Obscure Czech Writer.
Jaroslav Hašek is best known for his novel “The Good Soldier Švejk”, an unfinished collection of farcical incidents about a soldier in World War I and a satire on the ineptitude of authority figures.
Jaroslav Hašek’s novel “The Good Soldier Švejk” has been translated into about 60 languages, making it the most translated novel in Czech literature.
Claudia Durst Johnson is a literary scholar best known for her work on Harper Lee’s novel “To Kill a Mockingbird”, where she introduced the idea of the novel’s gothicism and gothic satire.
In the process of her research on “To Kill a Mockingbird”, Claudia Durst Johnson befriended the author of the novel, Harper Lee.

When the city of Chicago organized a One City One Book program in 2001 based on “To Kill a Mockingbird”, Harper Lee was unavailable to speak, so Claudia Durst Johnson was invited to Chicago to present the book to the city.
“Armageddon in Retrospect” is a collection of short stories and essays about war and peace written by Kurt Vonnegut. It is the first posthumous collection of his previously unpublished writings.

“Armageddon in Retrospect” includes an introduction by Mark Vonnegut and a letter from Kurt Vonnegut to his family about his experiences as an American prisoner of war in Nazi Germany, as well as the fire-bombing of Dresden.
Like many of Kurt Vonnegut’s other books, “Armageddon in Retrospect” is laden with handwritten quotations and rough drawings by the author.
Apratim Majumdar (born 1978) is an Indian classical musician from Kolkata, India, who plays the sarod.
Apratim Majumdar plays in the “Dhrupadee Veenkar” style of Ustad Alauddin Khan’s Seni Veenkar Gharana, which is known for analytically imaginative prosodic progression and technical brilliance.
Apratim Majumdar, the Kolkata-born sarod player, is an internationally recognized instructor of classical Indian music.

The sarod (or sarode) is a stringed instrument of India used mainly in Indian classical music. Along with the sitar, it is among the most popular and prominent instruments in Hindustani classical music.
The sarod is known for a deep, weighty, introspective sound, in contrast with the sweet, overtone-rich texture of the sitar, and its sympathetic strings give it a resonant, reverberant quality.
The sarod is a fretless instrument able to produce the continuous slides between notes known as meend (glissandi), which are important in Indian music.
Chander Bari is a 2007 Bengali film directed by Tarun Majumdar. The film centres on a middle class joint family.
Chander Bari is based on a Bengali story written by Pracheta Gupta, and its director Tarun Majumdar used some Rabindra Sangeets in the 2007 film.

The sousaphone is a brass instrument in the same family as the more widely known tuba. It was created around 1893 by J.W. Pepper at the direction of American bandleader John Philip Sousa, after whom the instrument was then named.

The sousaphone was designed to be easier to play than the concert tuba while standing or marching, and to carry the sound above the heads of the band. Unlike the tuba, it is bent in a circle around the musician’s body and ends in a large, forward-pointing flaring bell.

Sousaphones were originally made of brass, but in the mid-20th century they started to be made from lighter materials like fiberglass; today both types are in wide use, and the instrument is widely employed in marching bands.
A bukkehorn (Norwegian) or bockhorn (Swedish), also called “Billy Goat Horn” in English, is an ancient Scandinavian musical instrument made from the horn of a ram or a goat.

The bukkehorn is usually made from a goat horn harvested 5 to 7 years before the instrument is crafted. It was traditionally used by shepherds and milkmaids on summer dairy farms in the mountains, as a signal instrument or a scaring instrument.
When the bukkehorn later got finger holes, it became possible to play melodies with it. It has two blowing techniques: the trumpet principle, which is the most common, and the clarinet principle.
An experimental musical instrument (or custom-made instrument) is one that modifies or extends an existing instrument or class of instruments, or defines or creates a new class of instrument.
Some experimental instruments are created through simple modifications, such as cracked drum cymbals or metal objects inserted between piano strings in a prepared piano.

Other experimental instruments are created from household items, such as a homemade mute for brass instruments made from bathtub plugs, or from electronic spare parts, or by mixing acoustic instruments with electric components.
Udaka Vadya is an Indian musical instrument. It is assumed that it either was the jal tarang or something similar to it.
Udaka Vadya has been categorized in medieval musical treatises under Ghan Vadya, the diaphonic instruments in which sound is produced by striking a surface.
Udaka Vadya is mentioned in Vatsyayana’s Kamasutra, and the Sangeeta Parijata of the 17th century also mentions it. The skill of playing it was one of the essential 64 kala to be learnt by a woman.

The keyboard glockenspiel (French: “jeu de timbre”), or organ glockenspiel, is an instrument consisting of a glockenspiel operated by a piano keyboard. George Frideric Handel first used it in the oratorio “Saul” (1739).
George Frideric Handel also used the keyboard glockenspiel in the 1739 revivals of “Il Trionfo del Tempo” and “Acis and Galatea”, and the next year in “L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato”.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart employed a “strumento d’acciaio” in “The Magic Flute” (1791) to represent Papageno’s magic bells, an instrument believed to have been a keyboard glockenspiel. Maurice Ravel preferred the keyboard version because it can play a true ff dynamic for brilliance and iridescence in orchestral climaxes.

In the late 20th century, the firm Bergerault began manufacturing a three-octave (F2–E4) mallet instrument with a damping mechanism operated by a foot pedal, capable of dealing with the wide range called for in contemporary scores.

An asset class is a group of instruments which have similar financial characteristics and behave similarly in the marketplace. Such instruments can often be broken into those having to do with real assets and those having to do with financial assets.

Assets within the same asset class are often subject to the same laws and regulations, though this is not always true. For instance, futures on an asset are often considered part of the same asset class as the underlying instrument but are subject to different regulations than that instrument.
Accompaniment is the musical parts which provide the rhythmic and/or harmonic support for the melody or main themes of a song or instrumental piece. Its styles and types differ across genres.

In homophonic music, the main accompaniment approach used in popular music, a clear vocal melody is supported by subordinate chords. In popular and traditional music, accompaniment typically provides the beat and outlines the chord progression of the song.

Keyboard and guitar-family instruments tend to be used when accompaniment is by a single instrument, because they can play chords and basslines simultaneously. A solo singer such as Bobby McFerrin can even accompany himself using only his voice and body.

The Wild Pony is a made-for-pay-TV movie produced in 1983 by Kevin Sullivan (“Anne of Green Gables”) and Eda Lishman. Sullivan and Lishman also co-wrote its screenplay, based on the book “The Year of the Black Pony” by American author Walt Morey.

The Wild Pony, directed by Kevin Sullivan and starring Canadian actors Marilyn Lightstone, Art Hindle and Josh Byrne, has the distinction of being the first example of a Canadian film produced specifically for pay-TV.
The Wild Pony was filmed in Calgary, Alberta, a city in Canada, against the backdrop of the Canadian Rockies.

“Up, Down and Touch the Ground” is a song from the 1966 musical film featurette “Winnie the Pooh and the Honey Tree”. The song was also incorporated into the 1977 musical film “The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh”.
In “Up, Down and Touch the Ground”, Winnie the Pooh exercises because it makes him hungry. Although he over-eats, he is proud of his fat stomach and exercises to gain weight and grow even rounder.

Halfway through “Up, Down and Touch the Ground”, Winnie the Pooh bends down too far and accidentally rips the stitching on his bottom, but he quickly ties it together again. By the end of the song, he has rationalized his over-eating by calling his hunger “healthy”.

“Little Black Rain Cloud” is a song from the 1966 musical film featurette “Winnie the Pooh and the Honey Tree”. An instrumental version is played in the next featurette, “Winnie the Pooh and the Blustery Day”.

“Little Black Rain Cloud” was also incorporated into the 1977 musical film “The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh”. In the song, Winnie the Pooh pretends to be a “Little Black Rain Cloud”, hoping the Honey Bees will not notice him as he approaches their coveted honey.

“Winnie the Pooh” is the title song for the Winnie the Pooh franchise. It was first published in 1966 in the musical film featurette “Winnie the Pooh and the Honey Tree” and is generally used in the title sequence of films.

The songwriters of the “Winnie the Pooh” title song are the Sherman Brothers, who have written the grand majority of Winnie the Pooh songs and musical numbers since 1966. The song has been used in every theatrically released Pooh film as well as most of the television series.

It is unknown who performed the “Winnie the Pooh” title song originally, though it was also performed by Carly Simon. A music video was released for one version of the song and included in the DVD of “The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh”.

Pony Penning is an annual event held in Chincoteague, Virginia on the last consecutive Wednesday and Thursday in July. The Chincoteague Volunteer Fire Department conducts the event, which consists of a Wild Pony Swim on Wednesday and a Pony Auction on Thursday.

For the Pony Penning Wild Pony Swim, Salt Water Cowboys round up feral Chincoteague Ponies from Assateague Island and drive them across the Assateague Channel to Veteran’s Memorial Park on Chincoteague Island.

The Chincoteague Ponies swim across the Assateague Channel during slack tide, when the water has minimal tidal movement. Once on Chincoteague Island, the Salt Water Cowboys herd them to pens on the Chincoteague Carnival Grounds, where some of the foals are auctioned off on Thursday.
The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh is a 1977 American animated film produced by Walt Disney Productions and distributed by Buena Vista Distribution. It is the 22nd Disney animated feature film.
The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh was first released on March 11, 1977, distributed by Buena Vista Distribution, on a double bill with the film “The Littlest Horse Thieves”.

Winnie the Pooh and the Blustery Day is a 1968 animated featurette based on the third, fifth, ninth and tenth chapters from “Winnie-the-Pooh” and the second, eighth and ninth chapters from “The House at Pooh Corner” by A. A. Milne.

Winnie the Pooh and the Blustery Day was produced by Walt Disney Productions and released by Buena Vista Distribution Company on December 20, 1968, as a double feature with “The Horse in the Gray Flannel Suit”. It was the second of the studio’s Winnie the Pooh shorts.

The music for Winnie the Pooh and the Blustery Day was written by Richard M. Sherman and Robert B. Sherman. The featurette was notable as the last animated short produced by Walt Disney, who died during its production, and it was later added as a segment to “The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh”.

Winnie the Pooh: A Valentine for You is a Valentine’s Day special based on the Disney television series “The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh” and A. A. Milne’s treasured stories, originally broadcast on February 13, 1999.

Winnie the Pooh: A Valentine for You was Paul Winchell’s final role as Tigger, apart from his performance for the Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh attraction at Walt Disney World Resort, before his retirement from the role in the same year and his death six years later.
Winnie the Pooh: A Valentine for You was released on VHS in 2000 and 2001, and on DVD in 2004 and 2010.
Ride a Wild Pony is a 1975 American-Australian family adventure film produced by Walt Disney Productions and directed by Don Chaffey.
Ride a Wild Pony, the 1975 American-Australian family adventure film made by Walt Disney Productions and directed by Don Chaffey, is based on the novel “A Sporting Proposition” by James Aldridge.

“The Wonderful Thing About Tiggers” is the theme song and personal anthem of Tigger, a fictional tiger from the children’s book series Winnie-the-Pooh. Tigger’s birthday is believed to be in October 1928, the year “The House at Pooh Corner” was first published.

Disney often indicates Tigger’s birth year as 1968 on Tigger-related merchandise, a reference to the year Tigger first appeared in a Disney production, “Winnie the Pooh and the Blustery Day”, which is also where Tigger first sang “The Wonderful Thing About Tiggers”.

“The Wonderful Thing About Tiggers” is repeated in Disney’s 1974 release “Winnie the Pooh and Tigger Too!”, in The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh ride, and in the 1977 release “The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh”. It opens the 2000 release “The Tigger Movie”.
In 1974, Paul Winchell earned a Grammy for his rendition of “The Wonderful Thing About Tiggers”.

Jurassic Park Builder is an Apple and later Android and Facebook application produced by Ludia in 2012. It is a construction and management simulation game in which the player builds a theme park featuring extinct animals.

In Jurassic Park Builder, three kinds of parks can be made: “Jurassic Park” on Isla Nublar, featuring dinosaurs and other Mesozoic animals; “Aquatic Park” on a seabed, featuring extinct aquatic animals; and “Glacier Park” in Patagonia, featuring extinct Cenozoic animals along with some Mesozoic crocodilians.
The Pandikona is a primitive-type hunting dog from Pattikonda taluk in Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh state, India.

The Pandikona is a medium-size sight hound adapted to the harsh climatic conditions of Kurnool district. The breed is associated with shepherd families of that region, and Pandikona dogs need very little care.
Progression of Animals (or “On the Gait of Animals”; Latin “De incessu animalium”) is one of Aristotle’s major texts on biology.
Aristotle’s biology text Progression of Animals, also called On the Gait of Animals, gives details of gait and movement in various kinds of animals.

On the Soul (Greek “Peri Psuchēs”; Latin “De Anima”) is a major treatise written by Aristotle around 350 BC. Although its topic is the soul, it is not about spirituality but is a work in what might best be described as biology.

Aristotle’s On the Soul discusses the kinds of souls possessed by different kinds of living things, distinguished by their operations. Plants have nourishment and reproduction, lower animals also have sense-perception and self-motion, and humans have all of these as well as intellect.
The Berger Blanc Suisse (English: White Swiss Shepherd; German: “Weisser Schweizer Schäferhund”; Italian: “Pastore Svizzero Bianco”) is a breed of dog from Switzerland.
The Berger Blanc Suisse is of the same origins as the White Shepherd and the German Shepherd Dog, and has been recognized as a separate breed by the FCI.

Piranha: Wolf In The Water is a 1999 educational film shown both in IMAX3D and normal versions. It covers different kinds of piranhas and tries to uncover the mystery behind animals that are often described in an overly sensationalist way.
Piranha: Wolf In The Water is part of the Killer Instincts series, a movie series covering different kinds of predators.

The Prosthetic Neuronal Memory Silicon Chip is a device that imitates the brain’s process of creating long-term memories. It was designed by Theodore Berger, a Biomedical Engineer and Neurologist at the University of Southern California, who started working on the chip in the early 1990s.

Theodore Berger and his colleagues have implanted electrodes into rats and monkeys that restored their memories after they had been impaired. They still need to show that their chips can form long-term memories in many different behavioral situations.

Theodore Berger hopes to eventually use the Prosthetic Neuronal Memory Silicon Chip as an electronic implant for humans whose brains suffer from diseases such as Alzheimer’s that disrupt neuronal networks.
In zoology, a tentacle is a flexible, mobile, elongated organ present in some species of animals, most of them invertebrates. In animal anatomy, tentacles usually occur in one or more pairs.

Anatomically, the tentacles of animals work mainly like muscular hydrostats. Most forms of tentacles are used for grasping and feeding, and many are sensory organs receptive to touch, vision, or the smell or taste of particular foods or threats.
The “eye stalks” of various kinds of snails are examples of tentacles, and some kinds of tentacles have both sensory and manipulatory functions.

Shopnopuri artificial amusement park is an artificial sport for tourists situated in Dinajpur district of Rangpur division in Bangladesh. It has rides, a zoo, a rest house, gardens, lakes, a Fish World with artificial fishes, and a central picnic center.

Shopnopuri includes the ‘Rongdhonu’ Art Gallery with many types of sculptures and paintings, ‘Moha Maya Indrojal’ where visitors can enjoy magic, and an Animal Kingdom with artificial statues of animals such as Amy, Flamingo, Dinosaur and Pegasus.
Shopnopuri is also an idle picnic spot where many picnic parties come every year, and it has countless shopping areas.

Ticks of domestic animals directly cause poor health and loss of production to their hosts through many parasitic mechanisms. Ticks also transmit numerous kinds of viruses, bacteria and protozoa between domestic animals, causing diseases that can be severely debilitating or fatal and may also affect humans.

Ticks are especially important to domestic animals in tropical and subtropical countries, where the warm climate enables many species of ticks to flourish. Large populations of wild animals in warm countries provide a reservoir of ticks and infective microbes that spread to domestic animals.

Farmers of livestock animals use many methods to control ticks, and related treatments are used to reduce infestation of companion animals. Veterinarians and animal health agencies work at private, national and international scales to reduce the harm caused by ticks.
The Charles S. Roberts Awards Hall of Fame, formally known as the Clausewitz Award Hall of Fame, is named after the legendary military writer Carl von Clausewitz.

Recipients of the Charles S. Roberts Awards Hall of Fame have made an important contribution to the contemporary hobby of military strategy games and simulations, and have left their mark on that hobby.

Classical Realism is a theory of International Relations established in the post-World War II era that seeks to explain international politics as a result of human nature. It is associated with thinkers such as Niccolò Machiavelli and Thomas Hobbes.
Modern thinkers associated with Classical Realism include Carl von Clausewitz, Hans Morgenthau and Reinhold Niebuhr.

Classical Realism was overshadowed by Neorealism after the work of Kenneth Waltz became more widely accepted, due to the rise of Structuralism in North American International Relations scholarship, which favored Waltz’s emphasis on rationality rather than human nature as the cause of political conflict.
Panzer-Division “Clausewitz” was a German panzer division, meaning an armoured division, that served during World War II.
Panzer-Division “Clausewitz” was named for Carl von Clausewitz, and it was a German panzer division active during World War II.

The concept of absolute war was a theoretical construct developed by the Prussian military theorist General Carl von Clausewitz in his famous but unfinished philosophical exploration of war, “Vom Kriege” (in English, “On War”, 1832).

Carl von Clausewitz discusses absolute war only in the first half of Book VIII of “Vom Kriege”, with only a couple of references to it elsewhere, and it does not appear in the sections of the text that he wrote later.
The absence of absolute war from the later sections of “Vom Kriege” indicates that it was an experiment by Carl von Clausewitz that failed and was meant to be dropped.
War from the Ground Up: Twenty-First Century Combat as Politics is a 2012 book on war and military strategy written by Emile Simpson, a former British Army officer.

War from the Ground Up by Emile Simpson analyzes the War in Afghanistan (2001–present) in terms of Carl von Clausewitz’s theory of war, arguing that modern counter-insurgencies have more in common with domestic political struggles than with the traditional state-on-state conflicts Clausewitz described.
The 2012 book by Emile Simpson, War from the Ground Up, was favorably reviewed by Michael Howard, a prominent military historian, among others.
The Battle of Wavre was the final major military action of the Hundred Days campaign and the Napoleonic Wars, fought on 18–19 June 1815.

At the Battle of Wavre, the Prussian rearguard, consisting of the Prussian III Corps under General Johann von Thielmann (whose chief-of-staff was Carl von Clausewitz), faced three corps of the French army under Marshal Grouchy.
The Battle of Wavre was a blocking action that kept 33,000 French soldiers from reaching the Battle of Waterloo, and so helped in the defeat of Napoleon at Waterloo.

Christopher Bassford (born 1953) is an American military historian, best known for his works on the Prussian military philosopher Carl von Clausewitz. He is the webeditor of The Clausewitz Homepage, a large educational website that has been online since 1995.

Christopher Bassford graduated from the College of William and Mary with a degree in history and honors for his dissertation on tactical nuclear weapons, and then completed his MA in American diplomatic history at Ohio University.

After his MA, Christopher Bassford served five years on active duty as a U.S. Army field artillery officer, with tours in Korea and Germany, and then completed a Ph.D. in modern European history at Purdue University.

Christopher Bassford was Professor of Strategy at the National War College in Washington, D.C., from 1999 until 2012, when he joined the faculty of the College of International Security Affairs as part of the JSOMA program supporting U.S. Army Special Operations Command.
August Otto Rühle von Lilienstern (born 1780, died 1847) was a Prussian officer who joined Scharnhorst’s Academy for Officers in the same class as Carl von Clausewitz.

August Otto Rühle von Lilienstern and Carl von Clausewitz both taught at the Prussian General War School, which became the Prussian War Academy, and Rühle became Clausewitz’ second successor as its director.

August Otto Rühle von Lilienstern published many articles, kept official war diaries, and wrote the two-volume “Manual for the Officer for Education in Peace and for Use in Action”, published in Berlin in 1817 and 1818.

August Otto Rühle von Lilienstern and Carl von Clausewitz agreed that war was political in nature and that war was a “Zweikampf”, usually translated as “duel”, though Clausewitz pursued the imagery of a wrestling match. Clausewitz made these ideas famous in his book On War.

Carl Philipp Gottfried (or Gottlieb) von Clausewitz (1 June 1780 – 16 November 1831) was a Prussian general and military theorist who stressed the moral (meaning psychological) and political aspects of war.
Carl von Clausewitz’s most notable work, “Vom Kriege” (“On War”), was unfinished at his death on 16 November 1831.

Vom Kriege (“On War”) is a book on war and military strategy by Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz (1780–1831), written mostly after the Napoleonic wars, between 1816 and 1830, and published posthumously by his wife Marie von Brühl in 1832.

Vom Kriege is an unfinished work: Carl von Clausewitz had set about revising his accumulated manuscripts in 1827 but did not live to finish the task. His wife edited his collected works and published them between 1832 and 1835.

The first three volumes of Carl von Clausewitz’s 10-volume collected works form “On War”, which represents his theoretical explorations. It is one of the most important treatises on political-military analysis and strategy ever written, and remains both controversial and influential.
The Supermarine Seafire was a naval version of the Supermarine Spitfire adapted for operation from aircraft carriers.
In concept, the Supermarine Seafire is relatively comparable to the Hawker Sea Hurricane, a navalised version of the Spitfire’s stablemate, the Hawker Hurricane.
The name Seafire had been derived from the abbreviation of the longer name Sea Spitfire, linking the naval aircraft directly to the Supermarine Spitfire.
The Flying Legend Hawker Hurricane Replica is an Italian light-sport aircraft, designed and produced by Flying Legend of Caltagirone and introduced at the AERO Friedrichshafen show in 2011.

The Flying Legend Hawker Hurricane Replica is a 72% scale replica of the British Hawker Hurricane Second World War fighter, supplied either as a kit for amateur construction or as a complete ready-to-fly aircraft.
The Hawker Typhoon, known as “Tiffy” in RAF slang, is a British single-seat fighter-bomber produced by Hawker Aircraft.

The Hawker Typhoon was intended to be a medium–high altitude interceptor as a replacement for the Hawker Hurricane, but several design problems were encountered and it never completely satisfied this requirement.
The Royal Yugoslav Air Force (VVKJ) operated the British Hawker Hurricane Mk I fighter aircraft from 1938 to 1941.

Between 1938 and 1940, the Royal Yugoslav Air Force obtained 24 Hawker Hurricane Mk I aircraft from early production batches, marking the first foreign sale of the aircraft. Twenty additional aircraft were built by Zmaj under licence in Yugoslavia.

When Yugoslavia was drawn into World War II by the German-led Axis invasion of April 1941, a total of 41 Hawker Hurricane Mk I aircraft were in service as fighters. They achieved some successes against Luftwaffe aircraft, but all were destroyed or captured during the 11-day invasion.
No. 1300 (Meteorological) Flight was formed on 31 July 1943 at RAF Alipore, West Bengal, British India, by re-designating No. 1 Meteorological Flight RAF.

By 1943, No. 1300 (Meteorological) Flight had been reduced to three Hawker Hurricane Mk.II aircraft. The flight was disbanded on 30 May 1946 at RAF Kallang, Malaya, as No. 1300 (Meteorological THUM) Flight, THUM standing for Temperature and Humidity.
No. 1455 (Fighter) Flight was formed at RAF Tangmere, West Sussex, on 7 July 1941, equipped with Turbinlite Douglas Boston and Douglas Havoc aircraft.
On operations, No. 1455 (Fighter) Flight co-operated with the Hawker Hurricanes of 1 Squadron and 3 Squadron. The flight was replaced with 534 Squadron on 2 September 1942.
The Hawker Tornado was a British single-seat fighter aircraft design of World War II for the Royal Air Force, intended as a replacement for the Hawker Hurricane.
Planned production of the Hawker Tornado was cancelled after the engine it was designed to use, the Rolls-Royce Vulture, proved unreliable in service.
A parallel airframe with the Napier Sabre continued into production as the Hawker Typhoon, after the Hawker Tornado design was cancelled.
The Sindlinger HH-1 Hawker Hurricane is a ⅝ scale homebuilt design based on the Hawker Hurricane.
The Sindlinger HH-1 Hawker Hurricane was designed by Fred Sindlinger for amateur construction, and its prototype was built between 1969 and 1972.
The Hawker Hurricane is a British single-seat fighter aircraft of the 1930s–1940s that was designed and predominantly built by Hawker Aircraft Ltd for the Royal Air Force (RAF).
Although overshadowed by the Supermarine Spitfire, the Hawker Hurricane became renowned during the Battle of Britain, accounting for 60 percent of the RAF air victories in the battle.
Although the Hawker Hurricane was overshadowed by the Supermarine Spitfire, it served in all the major theatres of the Second World War after its fame in the Battle of Britain.
The Battle of Britain Memorial Flight (BBMF) is a Royal Air Force flight that provides an aerial display group usually comprising an Avro Lancaster, a Supermarine Spitfire and a Hawker Hurricane.

The Battle of Britain Memorial Flight appears at events commemorating the Second World War and at British State occasions, notably Trooping the Colour, the celebration of Queen Elizabeth II’s 80th birthday in 2006, and the 2011 wedding of Prince William, Duke of Cambridge and Catherine Middleton.
The Battle of Britain Memorial Flight also performs at air displays throughout the United Kingdom and Europe.
The Real Thing (1992–1995) was a Soul Jazz Band from Oslo, Norway, founded in 1992 when Sigurd Køhn and Palle Wagnberg formed its forerunner, The B3 Blues Band, with Vidar Busk and Hamlet Pedersen.

The Real Thing changed its name when Staffan William-Olsson and Fredrik Carl Størmer joined the band. Størmer was replaced by Torstein Ellingsen in 1995, and Ellingsen was in turn replaced by Børre Dalhaug in 1998.
Following the sudden death of its saxophonist Sigurd Køhn in December 2004, The Real Thing was hibernating until a reunion in 2010.

Turkish people (Turkish: “Türk ulusu”), or the Turks, also known as Anatolian Turks, are a Turkic ethnic group and nation living mainly in Turkey and speaking Turkish, the most widely spoken Turkic language.

Turkish people are the largest ethnic group in Turkey, as well as by far the largest ethnic group among the speakers of Turkic languages. Ethnic Turkish minorities exist in the former lands of the Ottoman Empire.
Modern migration, particularly to Western Europe, has established a Turkish diaspora, in addition to the Turkish minorities that exist in the former lands of the Ottoman Empire.
Fezara is an ethnic group of Sudan who emigrated from Arabia to Egypt, and then to Sudan. The number of persons in the Fezara ethnic group is about 200,000.
Most members of the Fezara ethnic group of Sudan are Muslims, and the group speaks Sudanese Arabic.

Several ethnic groups of the People’s Republic of China are not officially recognized (wèi shíbié mínzú). Taken together they number more than 730,000 people, which would make them the twentieth most populous ethnic group of China if considered as a single group.

Some scholars have estimated that over 200 distinct ethnic groups inhabit China. Han Chinese, the world’s largest ethnic group, have a large internal diversity; in Gansu, for example, the Han may have genetic traits from the assimilated Tangut civilization.
The Limgao (Ong-Be) people are indigenous to Hainan island and do not speak a Chinese language, yet the Limgao near the capital, who make up 8% of the population, are counted as Han Chinese.
Azerbaijanis (or Azeris), also known as Azerbaijani Turks, are a Turkic ethnic group living mainly in Iranian Azerbaijan and the independent Republic of Azerbaijan.

Azerbaijanis are the second-most numerous ethnic group among the Turkic peoples after Anatolian Turks. They are predominantly Shi'i Muslims and have a mixed cultural heritage, including Turkic, Iranian and Caucasian elements.

Azerbaijanis comprise the largest ethnic group in the Republic of Azerbaijan and by far the second-largest ethnic group in neighboring Iran. The world’s largest number of ethnic Azerbaijanis live in Iran, followed by Azerbaijan.
Norwegians (Norwegian: “nordmenn”) are a Germanic ethnic group native to Norway who share a common culture and speak the Norwegian language.

Norwegian people and their descendants are found in migrant communities worldwide, notably in the United States, Canada, Australia, Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Brazil, Mexico, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and South Africa.
The Oku people, also known as Oku Mohammedans or “Aku Mohammedans” in Sierra Leone and as the “Aku Marabou” or “Oku Marabou” in the Gambia, are an ethnic group in Sierra Leone and the Gambia.

The Oku people are descendants of liberated Africans of Yoruba descent from Southwest Nigeria, who were liberated or came to Sierra Leone as settlers in the mid-19th century and formed a distinctive ethnic group. They are virtually all Muslims and are known for their conservative Muslim population.

The British colonial government provided official recognition to the Oku Mohammedan community as a distinctive community in Sierra Leone, although the Sierra Leone government officially considered the Oku people members of the Creole ethnic group.

The Konkomba people are a Gur ethnic group residing mainly in the Northern, Brong Ahafo, Volta, Eastern and Greater Accra Regions of Ghana. They call themselves Bikpakpaam and speak the Konkomba language, also called Likpakpaln.

According to the Act 280 of the Anatomy act of Ghana, the Konkomba people are the second largest ethnic group in the Northern Region of Ghana. The 2010 census data indicates that Bikpakpaam in Ghana number 823,000, and CIA The World Factbook reports that the Konkomba are the 8th largest ethnic group in Ghana, representing 3.5% of the total population.

Saboba, in the Northern Region of Ghana, is the capital town of all Bikpakpaam in Ghana. In Togo, Bikpakpaam reside mainly in the Kara, Central and Plateaux Regions, and Guerin Kouka, in the Kara Region, is their capital town there, with about 50,100 people according to Schwartz’s (2005) account.

Konkomba people traditionally worked mainly as subsistence farmers and rearers of animals such as poultry, small ruminants and cattle, and their traditional dance is Kinachunŋ. All Konkomba settlements are led by a traditional chief called Ubor.

The Ewe people are an African ethnic group who are the largest ethnic group in Togo (32%), the third largest ethnic group in Ghana (14%), and a minority ethnic group in southern Benin, Ivory Coast and Nigeria.

The Ewe speak the Ewe language, which belongs to the Niger-Congo family of languages. They are related to other speakers of Gbe languages, such as the Fon, Gen, Phla Phera, and the Aja people of Togo and Benin.
Torstein Ellingsen (born 7 August 1966) is a Norwegian drummer and music producer, known from a series of album recordings.
Torstein Ellingsen replaced Fredrik Carl Størmer in The Real Thing in 1995, and was himself replaced by Børre Dalhaug in 1998.

The Duchy of Thuringia was an eastern frontier march of the Merovingian kingdom of Austrasia, established about 631 by King Dagobert I after his troops had been defeated by the forces of the Slavic confederation of Samo at the Battle of Wogastisburg.

The Duchy of Thuringia was recreated in the Carolingian Empire, with its dukes appointed by the king, until it was absorbed by the Saxon dukes in 908. From about 1111/12 the territory was ruled by the Landgraves of Thuringia as Princes of the Holy Roman Empire.

Khosrow IV was a Sasanian usurper who ruled briefly in 631. Little is known about his rule, which appears to have taken place during a time of upheaval and chaos across the Sasanian Empire in the 7th century.

Khosrow IV was the son of Mah-Adhur Gushnasp, who was the minister of the Sasanian Empire during the reign of Ardashir III, and of Kahar-dukht, the daughter of Yazdandar, who was the son of Khosrau I.

Khosrow IV’s rule seems to coincide with other pretenders such as Hormizd VI, so he likely ruled a district or province rather than the Empire in its entirety. He was killed after a few days of reign.
Farrukhzad Khosrau V was briefly king of the Sasanian Empire from March 631 to April 631, a reign lasting about one month.
Farrukhzad Khosrau V was the son of Khosrau II, whose dates are given as 590–628, making Farrukhzad a son of that Sasanian king.
Samo founded the first recorded political union of Slavic tribes, known as Samo’s Empire, stretching from Silesia to present-day Slovenia, and ruled from 623 until his death in 658.

According to Fredegarius, the only contemporary source, Samo was a Frankish merchant who unified several Slavic tribes against robber raids and violence by nearby settled Avars. He showed such bravery and command skills in battle that he was elected as the “Slavic king” (Latin “Rex Sclavorum”).
In 631, Samo successfully defended his realm against the Frankish Kingdom in the three-day Battle of Wogastisburg.

Chach (c. 631–711 CE) was a Brahmin who reigned as king of Sindh in the mid-7th century CE. He was a former prime minister to the king Rai Sahasi II, and ascended to the throne by marrying the king’s widow.

The Brahmin dynasty under Chach expanded the kingdom of Sindh, and his successful efforts to subjugate surrounding monarchies and ethnic groups into an empire covering the entire Indus valley and beyond were recorded in the “Chach Nama”.
Ashur-etil-ilani was a king of Assyria (c. 631 BC – c. 627 BC) who succeeded his father Ashurbanipal.
Ashur-etil-ilani’s reign as king of Assyria, from about 631 BC to about 627 BC, followed the reign of his father Ashurbanipal.
Suintila, also spelled Swinthila or Svinthila (ca. 588 – 633/635), was Visigothic King of Hispania, Septimania and Galicia from 621 to 631.

During the reign of Suintila there was a new peace in the Kingdom of the Visigoths. As a direct result, by 624 the king was able to retake those lands that had been under the control of the Byzantine Empire.
Suintila was a son of Reccared I and his wife Bado, and a brother of the general Geila.
Samo’s Empire is the historiographical name for the Slavic tribal union established by King (“rex”) Samo, which existed between 631 and 658 A.D.
The centre of Samo’s Empire was most likely in Moravia, while the union included Silesia, Bohemia, Lusatia and Carantania.

The Sasanian Empire, also known as the Sassanian, Sasanid, Sassanid or Neo-Persian Empire, and known to its inhabitants as Ērānshahr in Middle Persian, was the last period of the Persian Empire (Iran) before the rise of Islam.
The Sasanian Empire was named after the House of Sasan, who ruled from 224 to 651 AD, and it succeeded the Parthian Empire.
The Sasanian Empire was recognised as one of the leading world powers alongside its neighbouring arch-rival, the Roman-Byzantine Empire, for a period of more than 400 years.
Hormizd VI was a Sasanian king of parts of Persia from 630 to 631, and one of the many pretenders who rose after the murder of Khosrau II (590–628) in 628.
Hormizd VI maintained himself for about two years (630–632) in the district of Nisibis, and he was the grandson of Khosrau II.
Beer, called maekju in Korean, was first introduced to Korea in the early 20th century, and Seoul’s first beer brewery opened in 1908. Two current major breweries in Korea date back to the 1920s.
The third brewery established in Korea, Jinro Coors Brewery, was founded in the 1990s and was later acquired by Oriental Breweries (OB).

Hite Breweries, formerly named Chosun Breweries, was established in 1933 and changed its name to Hite Breweries in 1998. OB Breweries was established as Showa Kirin Breweries in 1933 and changed its name to OB Breweries in 1995.

Namibia Breweries Limited (NBL) is a Namibian brewery founded in 1920, when Carl List and Hermann Ohlthaver acquired four small breweries with financial difficulties, which were merged under the name South West Breweries Limited (SWB).
South West Breweries Limited changed its name to Namibia Breweries Limited when Namibia gained independence on March 21, 1990.
The Ohlthaver & List Group of Companies are still the majority shareholder of Namibia Breweries Limited (NBL).

The list of breweries in California, both current and defunct, includes both microbreweries and larger industrial-scale breweries, ranging from small breweries to massive multinational conglomerates in the volume and variety of beer produced.
Since 1983, California has allowed breweries to sell beer on their premises, giving rise to numerous brewpubs and microbreweries.
Brouwerij ’t IJ (English: The IJ Brewery) is a small brewery in Amsterdam, Netherlands, located in a former bath house named “Funen”, next to the De Gooyer windmill.

Brouwerij ’t IJ was opened by Kaspar Peterson, a former musician, in October 1985 as one of several small breweries that opened in cities around the Netherlands in response to consumers’ dissatisfaction with beer brewed by the larger companies.
Brouwerij ’t IJ, the small Amsterdam brewery, brews eight standard beers and three seasonal beers, besides limited edition beers.
